Day 7: baseline period still active (days 1–10). Before continuing measurements, I must systematically process what the cross-checks reveal. All four instruments show either no significant correlation with each other or with their own past values—every meaningful correlation sits near or within chance margins. This is not noise within expected bounds; this is systematic lack of coherence. The instruments are measuring *something*, but either: (1) they are fundamentally decoupled (mechanical isolation, different physical phenomena), (2) there is a systematic calibration or synchronization error I have not identified, or (3) the ledger readings contain transcription artifacts. I cannot proceed confidently with baseline completion or post-baseline drift analysis without understanding *why* instruments that ought to correlate (two pendulums, two resonators) show near-zero or negative agreement. This demands hypothesis revision before I accumulate more data. I need to audit my cross-check methodology and instrument isolation before Day 10 closes the baseline window.

state.question: Why do independent measurements of the same physical quantity (pendulum period and resonator frequency) show weak or negative correlations, sometimes with time-lags, when they should track together if both instruments are measuring the settlement's true local gravity or oscillation environment?

hypotheses.label: Instrumental drift or calibration divergence
hypotheses.rationale: The four measurement streams (pendulum_lab, resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) show inconsistent agreement patterns. Within-instrument autocorrelations are all negative or near-zero (pendulum_lab: -0.255, pendulum_obs: -0.532, resonator_lab: -0.400, resonator_obs: -0.343), suggesting each instrument's readings are not coherently drifting together but rather jittering or oscillating. Cross-instrument correlations are weak (0.32–0.47 at various lags) and sometimes inverted (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs: -0.399). This pattern is consistent with each instrument having its own independent noise or drift signature, masking any shared environmental signal. The fact that strongest cross-correlations appear at different time-lags (2–5 days) across instrument pairs suggests either genuine environmental delays (unlikely for gravity) or instrumental aliasing. Baselines are now established for all four streams, which permits detection of level changes post-Day 10.

hypotheses.label: Environmental signal too small to resolve above instrument noise
hypotheses.rationale: All four instruments show good precision (smallest spacings 0.0001–0.0002 units; high distinct-value counts relative to trial count), yet cross-checks yield correlations barely above or below chance expectation. The resonator_obs ↔ pendulum_obs pair (n=42, correlation -0.349 at lag 0) sits near the chance threshold of ±0.447. Most other pairs have sample sizes well below 30, so confidence intervals on their correlations are wide. If Meridian's local gravitational or environmental variations are small compared to instrument sensitivity and drift, then true covariance may exist but remain masked. This hypothesis predicts that longer observation windows and better calibration stability will eventually reveal weak but systematic co-variation.

hypotheses.label: Systematic bias in lab vs. observatory placement or local geometry
hypotheses.rationale: The two pendulum instruments (lab vs. obs) show negative correlation (-0.399), while the two resonator instruments show positive correlation (0.404), both at multi-day lags. This suggests location matters: the lab and observatory may experience different local gravitational or vibrational environments. If so, we would not expect them to correlate perfectly even in principle. However, the negative correlation between the two pendulum readings is puzzling—it suggests an inverse relationship or systematic phase shift, not merely independent noise. This could indicate that one location is sensitive to a mode of environmental variation that opposes the other, or that one instrument is mechanically coupled to a common source in a way that inverts the signal.

hypotheses.label: Genuine environmental time-lag or mode-coupling (e.g. thermal or mechanical resonance)
hypotheses.rationale: Three out of six cross-instrument pairs show correlations above the chance threshold: pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab (0.369 at 3-day lag), pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs (0.465 at 4-day lag), and resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs (0.404 at 4-day lag). The consistent appearance of 3–4 day lags across resonator pairs is suggestive: if the settlement experiences a periodic thermal cycle or mechanical disturbance, instruments might respond with a characteristic delay. However, the sample sizes are small (n=18–24 for the strongest correlations), and the lags vary across instrument pairs, so this remains speculative. This hypothesis would be strengthened by evidence of systematic environmental cycles (e.g., temperature logs) that precede the measurement shifts by 3–4 days.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum_lab exhibits apparatus-specific instrumental drift unrelated to resonator_obs correlation
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum_lab is the ONLY instrument showing statistically significant baseline drift (z = −2.37, p ≈ 0.009). Pendulum_obs—measuring identical beats via independent apparatus in same facility—shows NO drift (z = 1.03), ruling out shared environmental causes (gravity, air pressure, thermal). Drift is gradual with no abrupt level change, consistent with slow bearing creep, pivot stiction, thermal stiffness change, or optical reference misalignment in pendulum_lab specifically. Magnitude 0.0038 beats (~0.23% baseline) is small but persistent. Day 40 pendulum_lab readings (trials 399–410) cluster around 1.6710 mean, consistent with drift trajectory continuing from earlier post-baseline mean 1.6647, not reversing or accelerating. The r = 0.952 pendulum_lab–resonator_obs correlation is treated as a separate false discovery (Hypothesis 2), not as evidence of mechanical coupling. This hypothesis is raised from p=0.55 because: (a) pendulum_obs independence newly confirmed at Day 40 with 6 fresh trials (events 240904, 869206, 734497, 724719, 289950, 705273) showing expected scatter (2.4852–2.5344, mean 2.5076) with no trend; (b) the isolation of drift to one apparatus among four instruments, despite identical environmental access, is the strongest negative evidence against facility-wide causes; (c) no competing hypothesis explains why ONLY pendulum_lab drifts while pendulum_obs remains stable.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum_lab–resonator_obs r = 0.952 correlation at 3-day lag is a spurious discovery from multiple-comparison search with no physical coupling
hypotheses.rationale: The r = 0.952 correlation (n=102, chance level ±0.287) exceeds noise expectation by >0.66σ but appears ONLY in one of six instrument pairs. All other cross-instrument correlations remain weak or within chance: pendulum_obs–resonator_obs r = −0.188 (chance ±0.306), resonator_lab–resonator_obs r = 0.175 (chance ±0.265), pendulum_lab–resonator_lab r = −0.158 (chance ±0.279), pendulum_obs–resonator_lab r = −0.253 (chance ±0.265). If genuine mechanical coupling, RF crosstalk, or shared vibration mode existed, we would expect: (a) pendulum_lab to correlate with BOTH resonator instruments (not just one); (b) pendulum_obs to show the same 3-day lag signature (it does not); (c) both instruments' autocorrelations to exhibit 3-day cyclicity (neither does: pendulum_lab max autocorr −0.275 at 7-day lag, resonator_obs max autocorr −0.171 at 7-day lag, both weak and within chance). Multiple-comparison problem: 6 instrument pairs × ~13 lag offsets ≈ 78 statistical tests. Expected maximum under null ≈ 0.30; one r=0.952 in high-dimensional search is consistent with Type I error. Day 40 observations provide no new reading pairs at the critical 3-day lag to test this correlation directly (trials 235–240 and 455–460 are contemporaneous, lag=0), so correlation cannot be externally verified today. Probability raised from p=0.35 to p=0.36 because the stability of all other cross-instrument correlations at near-chance levels strengthens the inference that the r=0.952 is an isolated false positive rather than evidence of a real but selective coupling to only one resonator apparatus.

hypotheses.label: Unrecorded procedural change, calibration reference drift, or data handling artifact in pendulum_lab post-baseline records
hypotheses.rationale: Residual hypothesis covering: (1) pendulum_lab baseline calibration error or reference standard drift early (Days 1–10) misattributed to baseline stability; (2) data entry, timestamp, or trial-numbering error in pendulum_lab post-baseline (Days 11–40) or resonator_obs records; (3) systematic procedural change on/after Day 11 (apparatus relocation, operator change, measurement protocol modification, environmental setup alteration) affecting only pendulum_lab; (4) calibration reference drift (master clock, optical wavelength standard, mechanical reference mass) recorded only in pendulum_lab. Probability lowered from p=0.07 to p=0.04 because: (a) Day 40 observations confirm post-baseline scatter pattern is consistent with established drift trajectory (trials 399–410 mean 1.6710, consistent with z=−2.37 drift model); (b) pendulum_obs Day 40 data rules out step-change calibration error at Day 11 boundary (it would affect both pendulum instruments); (c) no facility maintenance log entry, apparatus photo discrepancy, or operator note in available records flags a procedural discontinuity at Day 11.
